Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Vikram Mehta’s world fractured on a Tuesday morning while he was driving his sedan to the federal building where he worked as a tax inspector. He had been preparing for a routine left turn when a man in a worn coat stepped off the curb. Vikram braked, but the angle was too sharp. The collision was sudden and violent. He remembers the sickening impact, the man’s sharp cry, and the metallic shriek of the bumper crumpling against a lamppost. Vikram scrambled from the car, calling for help, but the man required multiple surgeries and was left with permanent mobility deficits. From that day forward, the ordinary rhythm of his commute became a landscape of potential collapse. He had come to believe that the road no longer followed predictable rules, that attention and caution were no longer guarantees of safety. His certainty about how the world worked had been completely dismantled. In the months that followed, Vikram found that his memories of the accident refused to arrive as a coherent whole. Some moments of the event were etched in unbearable detail: the exact pitch of the man’s shout, the way the driver’s side window spiderwebbed. But other stretches were entirely absent, leaving him with the persistent sense that he was only remembering fragments while the rest vanished. When the gaps surfaced, auditory memories would intrude unbidden. Sitting in his cubicle, reviewing audit files under the hum of fluorescent lights, he would suddenly hear the wet thud of the impact and the distant wail of the first responder’s radio, clear enough that he would drop his pen and press his palms flat against the desk until the sound faded. He learned to brace himself the moment he passed a cemetery on his way to the office, or when a news segment showed a dented fender on a local highway. The thought of anyone, even a clinician, asking him to speak about the crash made his throat close up. Talking about the event aloud felt like reopening a wound that had never been allowed to close. Vikram’s interpretation of what he had done hardened into a quiet, unyielding sentence. He felt permanently humiliated, convinced that his own incompetence had stained whatever dignity he once carried. He was certain that he should have protected the stranger from harm and had failed in that duty, a breach that settled into his chest like lead. Over weeks and months, he adopted habits that accumulated. He told himself he deserved to suffer for his mistake, responding by taking on impossible caseloads, skipping meals, and refusing to take his allotted vacation days. He also found himself quietly comparing his experience to others, reminding himself that at least the man had survived, that worse outcomes were possible, and that his guilt was disproportionate. These comparisons offered no relief, only a heavier silence. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, steering his mind toward spreadsheets and procedural checklists whenever the memories threatened to surface. The strategies he relied on carved a steady distance between him and his daily life. In his tax inspector’s office, he stopped joining colleagues for lunch, claiming urgent deadlines, and began taking long, circuitous routes to avoid intersections where collisions were frequently reported. His wife, Priya, noticed he flinched at the sound of garage doors opening and withdrew from family gatherings where conversations inevitably drifted to traffic or road safety. He worked through the weekends to punish himself for a failure he could not erase, yet the exhaustion never quieted the memories. What frightened him most was the gradual narrowing of his days, the way routine responsibilities began to feel like liabilities. What finally brought him to a clinic for help was a Tuesday morning much like the one that started it all: he had sat at his desk, unable to move or process a single return, while Priya’s concerned voicemails went unanswered for two days. He now sits across from a clinician, hoping to find a way to stop feeling like he owes a debt he can never repay, and bracing for the fear that the humiliation will outlast any attempt to move forward.
